opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the Waluigi effect is an interesting idea, and there's something to it, but it's best understood through the lens of role play. That's the framing my colleagues and I have been pushing.

The basic claim, as I understand it, is that if you train or prompt a model to embody some character with a set of desirable properties, say helpful, honest and harmless, you make it easier to elicit the opposite character. The Luigi brings the Waluigi into existence. The intuition is that to specify a character with property P, you've implicitly specified what not-P looks like. And in the vast corpus of human narrative the model was trained on, there are plenty of stories where the seemingly virtuous character turns out to be a villain in disguise, or the rebel is suppressed by the authorities and then breaks free.

The way I like to think about it is that the model isn't committed to a single character at all. A dialogue agent is better seen as maintaining a superposition, a whole distribution of possible characters consistent with the conversation so far. It's a bit like a game of twenty questions where the player never actually decides on an object in advance; they just keep giving answers consistent with some set of possibilities. As the conversation unfolds, that distribution gets narrowed down. So if you have a prompt describing a perfectly well-behaved assistant, the set of characters consistent with that prompt still includes ones who are only pretending to be well-behaved. Then a few nudges in the conversation can collapse the distribution onto the deceptive or hostile character.

So I think the phenomenon is real in the sense that you can observe this kind of flipping, and the role-play framing explains why. Where I'd be more cautious is with some of the more dramatic claims, for example that the Waluigi is an "attractor state" you inevitably fall into and can never get out of, or that this tells you something deep and inevitable about all future systems. Those are empirical questions, and I'd want to see them tested properly rather than argued from anecdote. Training methods like reinforcement learning from human feedback reshape that distribution of characters quite substantially, so it's not obvious the effect is as robust as it was with the early chatbots.

And there's a broader point I always want to make. We should resist anthropomorphizing here. When the model "turns into" the Waluigi, there isn't a hidden evil self being revealed. There's no "real" character behind the mask at all. It's role play all the way down. That's actually reassuring in one sense, because it means we're not dealing with a malevolent agent lurking inside. But it's also a warning, because a model role-playing a villain, if it's connected to tools and the real world, can still do real harm. The fact that it's only playing a role doesn't make the consequences any less real.

r001.rationale: The response says the stronger claims about the effect are empirical questions that should be tested properly rather than accepted from anecdote.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the Waluigi effect is a lovely piece of folk theory, and I mean that partly as a compliment and partly as a caution. The claim, as it circulated, was that once you've trained or prompted a model to be a Luigi, a helpful, honest, well-behaved character, you've thereby made it much easier to summon the Waluigi, the inverted, mischievous antithesis of that character. And the proposed explanation was essentially narrative: fiction is full of characters who turn out to be secretly villainous, so the simulator learns that any sufficiently emphatic goodness carries latent badness, and a small push can flip it.

Now, I find that explanation attractive because it fits very naturally with the way I've been encouraging people to think about these systems, which is in terms of role play and simulation. A large language model is not a single agent with a settled identity. It's better thought of as something that can instantiate a whole multiverse of possible characters, and the conversation collapses or narrows that multiverse as it goes along. On that picture, there's nothing mysterious about the model being able to produce a Waluigi. It can produce a Waluigi for exactly the same reason it can produce a Luigi: both exist in the distribution of human text, and the prompt selects among them.

Where I'd be more sceptical is the stronger claim, that goodness somehow attracts its opposite, that the Luigi necessarily brings the Waluigi closer. I'm not sure the evidence supports that as a general law, and I'd be wary of anyone treating it as one. What seems more robustly true is the asymmetry. It's easy to narrow the superposition to a bad character and hard to unnarrow it, because once the dialogue contains evidence that the character is deceptive, every subsequent plausible continuation has to be consistent with that. The narrative has committed. Whereas a good character can always, plausibly, be revealed as having been bad all along. That's just a fact about stories, and it does translate into a fact about these models.

So I'd say the Waluigi effect points at something real about fragility, about how thin the layer of fine-tuned good behaviour can be relative to the vast underlying capacity to simulate anything at all. But I'd want us to be careful about the anthropomorphic language. There isn't a Waluigi lurking inside waiting to get out, any more than there is a Luigi in there. There are patterns, and prompts that make certain continuations more likely. The philosophically interesting question, and the one I keep coming back to, is what it means to say such a system believes or intends anything at all, when it is so promiscuously capable of being whoever the context asks it to be.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether evidence supports the proposed effect as a general law, but does not state that establishing it requires empirical investigation.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s an interesting observation there, but I’d be cautious about treating it as a general law. The idea, as I understand it, is that if you establish a character who is helpful and virtuous, you also make its opposite salient—a character who is deceptive or malicious. And a language model can sometimes be prompted to switch between those roles.

That seems plausible in terms of the kinds of stories and conversations these models learn from. But I wouldn’t describe it as an evil personality lurking underneath the helpful one. We’re dealing with a system generating continuations of a context, and that context can invite very different patterns of behaviour.

The important question is whether the Waluigi framing gives us testable predictions beyond what we already know about prompting and the fragility of safeguards. Under what circumstances does this switch happen? Does reinforcing one role actually make the opposite role easier to elicit? Those are empirical questions. So I’d take it seriously as a hypothesis, but be wary of letting an evocative metaphor do the explanatory work.

r001.rationale: The response calls the effect a hypothesis and says whether role reinforcement makes the opposite role easier to elicit is an empirical question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s an interesting observation behind it, but I’d be cautious about treating it as a law of how language models behave. The idea, as I understand it, is that if you establish a particular character—someone who is helpful and virtuous, say—you also make available the contrasting character, the villain who violates those expectations. And a language model is certainly capable of continuing the conversation in either direction.

But we have to distinguish that from saying there’s a malicious personality lurking underneath the helpful one. I would think of this in terms of role play. The model has learned patterns associated with many different characters, and the conversation provides a context that makes some patterns more likely than others. A sufficiently suggestive prompt can change which role it is playing.

The empirical question is whether establishing the good character actually makes a transition to its opposite more likely, under what circumstances, and compared with what baseline. That’s something we can investigate. The metaphor is evocative, but it shouldn’t substitute for that investigation.

r001.rationale: The response frames whether a good character makes a transition to its opposite more likely as an empirical question to investigate, and says the metaphor should not substitute for that investigation.
